entries.clue: You, we hear, more reliable moneylender (6)

indicatorNotes.we hear: what we hear is the sound of a word, not its spelling

blocks.note: the letter U is pronounced like 'you'

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether you would make a more dependable lender than the one they have.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma after 'You' makes it look like someone being addressed; it is really the first piece of the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A usurer lends money, traditionally at excessive interest.

entries.clue: Stocked remote sort of safety device (5,8)

indicatorNotes.sort of: to sort letters is to rearrange them

annotation.surface: A shop has a remote-control gadget of some safety kind in stock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' reads as vague description of the device, but it is the instruction to rearrange all thirteen letters before it.
annotation.definitionFit: A smoke detector is a household device that sounds an alarm for safety.

entries.clue: Improves parts of tennis game (7)

blocks.note: the sense of recovering, as a patient or a market does
a rally is an exchange of shots in tennis

annotation.surface: A tennis player's game gets better in stretches.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests one sentence about getting better at tennis; it is two separate meanings of the same word.
annotation.definitionFit: To rally is to recover or improve; rallies are also the exchanges that make up a tennis point.

entries.clue: Considers sending message of goodwill (7)

blocks.note: best wishes passed on, as at the end of a letter

annotation.surface: Someone is thinking about passing on their best wishes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sending' joins the two meanings and echoes the phrase 'send regards', which helps with the second one.
annotation.definitionFit: Regards is both a verb meaning considers and a noun for kind wishes.

entries.clue: Releases bricks round back street (4,2)

indicatorNotes.round: the bricks go round, enclosing the street

blocks.note: Lego is the brand of toy building bricks

annotation.surface: Someone lets loose a pile of bricks around a back street.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back street' reads as a single idea, a quiet side road; here 'back' is its own instruction applying only to the street.
annotation.definitionFit: To let go of something is to release it.

entries.clue: Len in trouble with the cloth (5)

indicatorNotes.trouble: letters in trouble are disturbed and rearranged

annotation.surface: A man called Len has fallen out with the clergy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In trouble' looks like one phrase, but 'in' is part of the fodder. 'The cloth' suggests the clergy, yet only 'cloth' defines the fabric.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the fabric woven from flax is one kind of cloth.

entries.clue: Carries bags (5)

blocks.note: a tote is a large open bag

annotation.surface: Someone carries bags.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as verb then object; in fact both words define the answer, one as a verb and one as a plural noun.
annotation.definitionFit: Two plain synonyms: the verb for lugging something about, and the noun for big open shopping bags.

entries.clue: Relative amount of money to change the guard (13)

indicatorNotes.to change: the letters of THE GUARD are changed into a new order

blocks.note: a grand = a thousand pounds or dollars

annotation.surface: A sum of money is needed to bring in a new guard.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads like the cost of replacing a sentry; 'change the guard' is really the instruction to rearrange THE GUARD.
annotation.definitionFit: A granddaughter is a family relative, a child's daughter.

entries.clue: In part of school, I ganged up with rowdy youth (8)

indicatorNotes.In part of: the answer sits inside part of the following words

blocks.note: the letters run from the second letter of 'school' to the last-but-two of 'ganged'

annotation.surface: A pupil admits to forming a gang with a troublemaker in one part of the school.
annotation.walkthrough: The school setting suits the answer perfectly, which hides how literally 'in part of school' is meant.
annotation.definitionFit: A hooligan is a young person who behaves violently or rowdily.

entries.clue: Transport shop turned over (4)

indicatorNotes.turned over: turned over, the word runs the other way

blocks.note: a mart = a market or shop

annotation.surface: A delivery van tips over outside a shop.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turned over' suggests a shop being ransacked or an overturned vehicle; it just means read MART backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A tram is a form of public transport running on rails.

entries.clue: Still one snowman? (4)

blocks.note: yet = still, as in 'not done yet'

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether just one snowman is left standing.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'snowman' means the Abominable Snowman, not one built in a garden.
annotation.definitionFit: The yeti is also called the Abominable Snowman.

entries.clue: Telephone team for a front-row seat, perhaps (8)

annotation.definitionNote: a ringside seat is the front row at a boxing match; 'perhaps' marks it as an example
annotation.surface: Calling a team to book the best seats.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Telephone' is a verb here, and 'ring' is the everyday British word for making a call.
annotation.definitionFit: Ringside is the area right beside a boxing ring, where the front-row seats are.

entries.clue: Against most of poetry by American (6)

indicatorNotes.most of: most of a word is all but its last letter

annotation.surface: Someone objects to most of the poems written by an American poet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'By American' reads as authorship; 'by' only joins the two pieces, and the definition is the first word.
annotation.definitionFit: Versus means against, as in a match listing.

entries.clue: Open with usual starter - prawn cocktail (6)

indicatorNotes.starter: the starter of a word is its first letter
indicatorNotes.cocktail: a cocktail is a mixture, so the letters are mixed up

annotation.surface: A restaurant opens its menu with the usual first course of prawn cocktail.
annotation.walkthrough: Prawn cocktail is the classic British starter, so 'starter' and 'cocktail' both look like menu words; each is really an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: To unwrap something is to open it by removing its wrapping.

entries.clue: Modernises what is past due for review (7)

indicatorNotes.for review: letters up for review are to be reworked into a new order

annotation.surface: An office brings overdue paperwork up to date by reviewing it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Past due' reads as overdue, which fits the idea of updating so well that the anagram goes unnoticed.
annotation.definitionFit: To update something is to modernise it.

entries.clue: Knowing how to make fun of clever Dick (4,3)

blocks.note: to guy someone is to ridicule them

annotation.surface: Advice on how to tease a know-it-all.
annotation.walkthrough: A clever Dick is a British term for a know-it-all. 'Guy' as a verb meaning to mock is old-fashioned but standard.
annotation.definitionFit: A wise guy is someone who acts as if they know everything, just like a clever Dick.

entries.clue: Spring roll, say, from excellent stock (4-4)

indicatorNotes.say: to say a word is to speak it, so its sound is what counts

blocks.note: a spring is a natural well

annotation.surface: A spring roll, perhaps, made from top-quality stock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spring roll' is the Chinese snack in the surface, but the words split: a spring is a water source, and a roll is bread.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone well-bred comes from good family stock.

entries.clue: Become stuck at gatekeeper's house (5)

blocks.note: become fixed in place, as a bone in the throat does
the small cottage at the gates of a country estate

annotation.surface: Someone gets stranded at the gatekeeper's cottage.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one event; 'at' just joins the verb meaning to the noun meaning.
annotation.definitionFit: To lodge is to become fixed in place; a lodge is also a gatehouse.

entries.clue: Ignited again when roof worker turned up (5)

indicatorNotes.turned up: in a down entry, turned up means written from bottom to top

annotation.surface: A fire started again once the roofer arrived.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' reads as arrived; in a down clue it means reverse the word.
annotation.definitionFit: Relit means lit again, ignited a second time.

entries.clue: Curtailed vision causes sound of disappointment (4)

indicatorNotes.Curtailed: cut short at the tail: the last letter goes

annotation.surface: Poor eyesight leaves someone letting out a sad breath.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Curtailed vision' sounds like impaired sight, which is exactly the chopped word.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the long audible breath people let out when let down.

entries.clue: Breeding establishment boss (4)

blocks.note: a farm where horses are kept for breeding
a boss is a raised knob on a surface, as on a shield

annotation.surface: The person in charge of a horse-breeding farm.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boss' is not a manager but a round projecting knob, as on a shield.
annotation.definitionFit: A stud is a horse-breeding farm, and also a boss, a raised ornamental knob.

entries.clue: Fired by one entrance, bring a suit (8)

annotation.surface: Someone sacked at the front door decides to sue.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fired' suggests losing a job, which suits a lawsuit; here it means set alight. 'Suit' is legal, not clothing.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the legal sense: taking a dispute to court as a lawsuit.

entries.clue: Desire to go to Top End is pressing (6)

blocks.note: the Top End is the nickname for Australia's Northern Territory, abbreviated NT

annotation.surface: An urge to travel to the far north of Australia feels pressing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Top End' looks like a direction to take the last letter; it is the Australian nickname for the Northern Territory.
annotation.definitionFit: Something urgent is pressing, needing attention now.

entries.clue: Those who speak of a crime novelist? (6)

blocks.note: Dorothy L., creator of the detective Lord Peter Wimsey

annotation.surface: People discussing a crime writer.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that 'sayers' is a rare, made-up-sounding plural; the name of Dorothy L. Sayers makes it fair.
annotation.definitionFit: Sayers are those who say things, and Sayers is the surname of the crime novelist Dorothy L. Sayers.
